what: Step 1: Generating Messages for Each Document
title: Structured Question Answering from PDFs
text: First, prepare list messages PDFs folder applying llm_message() prompt first five pages document. Even though gpt-6-luna can process much longer documents, limit input five pages demonstration purposes; introduction usually enough get first overview paper. Attach PDFs pdf_file() .media argument. providers support native PDF rendering (Claude, Gemini), file sent binary, preserving images, tables, formatting. providers text extracted automatically wrapped <pdf> tags prompt. Pass .text_extract = TRUE always force text extraction regardless provider:
code: files <- list.files("aipapers", full.names = TRUE, pattern = "\\.pdf$")  document_tasks <- files |>   map(\(f) llm_message(     "Below are the first 5 pages of a document.      Summarise the document based on the provided schema.",     .media = pdf_file(f, pages = 1:5)   ))

what: Step 2: Defining the Schema for Structured Output
title: Structured Question Answering from PDFs
text: define schema outlines expected data types field model’s responses. enables model return answers consistent, structured format converts directly tibble. field_chr() returns text, field_dbl() returns numbers, field_fct() restricts allowed categories via .levels argument. Setting .vector = TRUE field returns list values; keep flat structure document maps single-row tibble. name special field providing identifier schema.
code: document_schema <- tidyllm_schema(   name             = "DocumentAnalysisSchema",   Title            = field_chr("The full title of the provided document"),   Authors          = field_chr("A semicolon-separated list of authors"),   SuggestedFilename = field_chr("Suggest a filename in the format \"ReleaseYear_Author_etal_ShortTitle.pdf\". Use the publication year if available; otherwise, use XXXX."),   Type             = field_fct("Is the document a Policy Report or a Research Paper based on its style, structure, and purpose?",                                .levels = c("Policy", "Research")),   Empirics         = field_chr("A 100 word description of empirical methods used, including data collection, statistical techniques, or analysis methods mentioned."),   Theory           = field_chr("A 100 word outline of the primary theoretical framework or models discussed, if any."),   MainPoint        = field_chr("A one-sentence summary of the main point raised"),   Contribution     = field_chr("A short explanation of the main contributions claimed in the document"),   KeyCitations     = field_chr("The four most frequently cited or critical references in the first 5 pages") )

what: Step 3: Running the Analysis on a Sample Document
title: Structured Question Answering from PDFs
text: test setup, run analysis single document chat() schema:
code: example_task <- document_tasks[[1]] |>   chat(openai(.json_schema = document_schema,               .model       = "gpt-6-luna"))

what: Step 4: Extracting and Formatting the Results
title: Structured Question Answering from PDFs
text: get_reply_data() extracts model’s structured response: model returns named list matching schema, as_tibble() converts single row. can also inspect token usage: current gpt-6-luna batch pricing ($0.05 per million input $0.25 per million output tokens) per-document cost fraction cent; processing 25 papers folder cost 1.5 cents, folder 50 papers costs cents.
code: get_reply_data(example_task) ## $Title ## [1] "A Method to Link Advances in Artificial Intelligence to Occupational Abilities" ##  ## $Authors ## [1] "Edward W. Felten; Manav Raj; Robert Seamans" ##  ## $SuggestedFilename ## [1] "2018_Felten_etal_AI_Occupational_Abilities.pdf" ##  ## $Type ## [1] "Research" ##  ## $Empirics ## [1] "The study combines the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s AI Progress Measurement data with the US Department of Labor’s O*NET occupational database. For 16 AI categories, the authors scale different performance metrics, estimate progress trends using a common linear rate with metric-specific offsets, and set progress to zero where historical data are insufficient. Computer science PhD students help map AI categories to 52 O*NET abilities. The authors weight estimated ability effects by each ability’s importance and prevalence across nearly 1,000 occupations, then aggregate occupation scores. As a validation test, they correlate 2010–2015 scores with planned 2018 BLS definition revisions: the correlation is 0.074 (p = 0.041)." ##  ## $Theory ## [1] "The paper uses a skills- and abilities-based view of labor: an occupation is understood as a bundle of abilities, with each ability varying in importance and prevalence across jobs. Advances in particular AI domains may affect the abilities used in occupations, so mapping AI progress to abilities and then to occupational requirements provides a way to compare relative exposure. This framework complements approaches that predict future automation susceptibility at the occupation level and those emphasizing variation in tasks among workers with the same occupational title. It does not provide a formal model of labor-market adjustment or determine whether AI substitutes for or complements workers; either outcome may occur." ##  ## $MainPoint ## [1] "The authors propose a method for linking measured advances in specific AI domains to occupational abilities and aggregating those links to compare which occupations may be affected." ##  ## $Contribution ## [1] "The paper introduces a reproducible framework that combines historical AI performance trends with O*NET ability requirements, enabling researchers and policymakers to assess the relative exposure of occupations and industries to advances in particular AI technologies. It also offers an initial validation: occupations with higher impact scores were modestly more likely to be scheduled for updated BLS definitions." ##  ## $KeyCitations ## [1] "Frey and Osborne (2017), “The Future of Employment,” provides an occupation-level automation-susceptibility approach that this method complements. Arntz, Gregory, and Zierahn (2016), “The Risk of Automation for Jobs in OECD Countries,” highlights task variation within occupations. Autor and Handel (2013), “Putting Tasks to the Test,” supports describing labor through job tasks and skills. Brynjolfsson, Mitchell, and Rock (2018), “What Can Machines Learn, and What Does it Mean for the Occupations and Industries?,” is a related approach to assessing AI and occupational effects." get_metadata(example_task) ## # A tibble: 1 × 7 ##   model  timestamp           prompt_tokens completion_tokens total_tokens stream ##   <chr>  <dttm>                      <int>             <int>        <int> <lgl>  ## 1 gpt-6… 2026-10-02 15:20:13          4223              1051         5274 FALSE  ## # ℹ 1 more variable: api_specific <list>

what: Step 5: Scaling Up to a Whole Batch of Papers
title: Structured Question Answering from PDFs
text: confirming single-document analysis works, extend workflow process full batch. Batch APIs Anthropic OpenAI offer 50% savings compared single requests, batch rate limits separate standard per-model limits don’t affect regular quota. output send_batch() contains input message list plus batch metadata (batch_id attribute unique per-message identifiers). Batches processed within 24 hours; example completed 10 minutes. ⚠️ Note: Save RDS file disk. acts checkpoint, letting reload check batch status retrieve results across R sessions without resubmitting batch. text: use pdf_file() gemini() claude(), PDF sent binary rather extracted text. means model sees actual layout, tables, charts, scanned pages, just raw characters. text-workflows provider, pass .text_extract = TRUE pdf_file() force text extraction skip binary encoding entirely. large frequently reused documents can also upload provider’s servers upload_file() reference returned handle messages via .files. avoids re-sending binary every request. Provider file APIs often accept broader range formats beyond PDFs: Gemini supports video, audio, various document types; OpenAI accepts Office files (DOCX, PPTX, XLSX), source code, ZIP archives, . makes upload_file() useful workflows go beyond plain PDFs. title: Get Started
text: tidyllm built around message-centric interface. Interactions work message history created llm_message() passed verbs like chat(): API interactions follow verb + provider pattern: Verbs define action: chat(), embed(), send_batch(), check_batch(), fetch_batch(), list_batches(), list_models(), deep_research(), decide(), check_job(), fetch_job(), upload_file(), list_files(), file_info(), delete_file() Providers specify API: openai(), claude(), claude_cli(), codex_cli(), vibe_cli(), gemini(), ollama(), mistral(), groq(), deepseek(), voyage(), openrouter(), jev(), llamacpp(), azure_openai(), ellmer() Provider-specific functions like openai_chat() claude_chat() also work directly expose full range parameters API.
code: library(tidyllm)  conversation <- llm_message("What is the capital of France?") |>   chat(claude())  conversation ## Message History: ## system: ## You are a helpful assistant ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## user: ## What is the capital of France? ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## assistant: ## The capital of France is Paris. ## -------------------------------------------------------------- # Continue the conversation with a different provider conversation <- conversation |>   llm_message("What's a famous landmark in this city?") |>   chat(openai())  get_reply(conversation) ## [1] "A famous landmark in Paris is the Eiffel Tower."

title: Get Started
text: Attach images, PDFs, audio, video message using .media argument llm_message(). Pass single media object list :  Send multiple images one message passing list. list can also mix different media types; example, image alongside PDF audio file alongside chart. Gemini handles mixed-type lists flexibly: audio video, use audio_file() video_file(). Gemini supports natively; llama.cpp supports audio compatible models (Ultravox, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni); OpenRouter routes audio video underlying models accept :
code: # Single image image_description <- llm_message("Describe this picture. Can you guess where it was taken?",                                   .media = img("picture.jpeg")) |>   chat(openai(.model = "gpt-6-luna"))  get_reply(image_description) ## [1] "The picture shows a beautiful landscape with a lake, mountains, and a town nestled below. The area appears lush and green, with agricultural fields visible. This scenery is reminiscent of northern Italy, particularly around Lake Garda." llm_message("Compare these two charts.",             .media = list(img("chart_a.png"), img("chart_b.png"))) |>   chat(claude())  # Mixed types in one message llm_message("Does this figure match the results described in the paper?",             .media = list(img("figure.png"), pdf_file("paper.pdf", pages = 1:5))) |>   chat(gemini()) # Audio transcription or analysis llm_message("Transcribe and summarise this recording.",             .media = audio_file("interview.mp3")) |>   chat(gemini())  # Video understanding llm_message("Describe what happens in this clip.",             .media = video_file("demo.mp4")) |>   chat(gemini())

title: Get Started
text: Pass PDF pdf_file() attach .media. default file sent binary providers support native PDF rendering (Claude, Gemini), text automatically extracted fallback others: Restrict specific pages pages argument: large frequently reused documents, upload provider’s Files API reference handle message: File management verbs currently supported Claude, Gemini, OpenAI. Files uploaded stored specific provider’s servers; file uploaded Claude used Gemini OpenAI. Supported file types vary provider: Gemini accepts wide range including video, audio, images, PDFs, various document formats. OpenAI accepts 80+ formats including Office documents (PPTX, DOCX, XLSX), source code, ZIP archives, . Claude focuses PDFs images. Always check provider’s current documentation full list.
code: llm_message("Summarize the key points from this document.",             .media = pdf_file("die_verwandlung.pdf")) |>   chat(claude()) ## Message History: ## system: ## You are a helpful assistant ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## user: ## Summarize the key points from this document. ##  -> [pdf: die_verwandlung.pdf]  ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## assistant: ## The story centres on Gregor Samsa, who wakes up transformed ## into a giant insect. Unable to work, he becomes isolated ## while his family struggles. Eventually Gregor dies, and his ## relieved family looks ahead to a better future. ## -------------------------------------------------------------- pdf_file("report.pdf", pages = 1:5) report <- upload_file(claude(), .path = "annual_report.pdf")  llm_message("What are the key risks mentioned?", .files = report) |>   chat(claude())  # Manage uploaded files list_files(claude()) file_info(claude(), report) delete_file(claude(), report)

title: Get Started
text: tidyllm supports JSON schema enforcement models return structured, machine-readable data. Use tidyllm_schema() field helpers define schema: field_chr(): text field_dbl(): numeric field_lgl(): boolean field_fct(.levels = ...): enumeration field_object(...): nested object (supports .vector = TRUE arrays) Extract parsed result R list get_reply_data(): Set .vector = TRUE field_object() get outputs unpack directly data frame: ellmer package installed, can use ellmer type objects (ellmer::type_string(), ellmer::type_object(), etc.) directly field definitions tidyllm_schema() .json_schema argument.
code: person_schema <- tidyllm_schema(   first_name = field_chr("A male first name"),   last_name  = field_chr("A common last name"),   occupation = field_chr("A quirky occupation"),   address    = field_object(     "The person's home address",     street  = field_chr("Street name"),     number  = field_dbl("House number"),     city    = field_chr("A large city"),     zip     = field_dbl("Postal code"),     country = field_fct("Country", .levels = c("Germany", "France"))   ) )  profile <- llm_message("Imagine a person profile matching the schema.") |>   chat(openai(), .json_schema = person_schema)  profile ## Message History: ## system: ## You are a helpful assistant ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## user: ## Imagine a person profile matching the schema. ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## assistant: ## {"first_name":"Julien","last_name":"Martin","occupation":"Gondola ## Repair Specialist","address":{"street":"Rue de ## Rivoli","number":112,"city":"Paris","zip":75001,"country":"France"}} ## -------------------------------------------------------------- profile |> get_reply_data() |> str() ## List of 4 ##  $ first_name: chr "Julien" ##  $ last_name : chr "Martin" ##  $ occupation: chr "Gondola Repair Specialist" ##  $ address   :List of 5 ##   ..$ street : chr "Rue de Rivoli" ##   ..$ number : int 112 ##   ..$ city   : chr "Paris" ##   ..$ zip    : int 75001 ##   ..$ country: chr "France" llm_message("Imagine five people.") |>   chat(openai(),        .json_schema = tidyllm_schema(          person = field_object(            first_name = field_chr(),            last_name  = field_chr(),            occupation = field_chr(),            .vector    = TRUE          )        )) |>   get_reply_data() |>   bind_rows() ##   first_name last_name          occupation ## 1      Alice   Johnson  Software Developer ## 2     Robert  Anderson    Graphic Designer ## 3      Maria  Gonzalez      Data Scientist ## 4       Liam  O'Connor Mechanical Engineer ## 5     Sophia       Lee      Content Writer

title: Get Started
text: Common arguments like .model, .temperature, .json_schema can set directly verbs like chat(). Provider-specific arguments go provider function: argument appears chat() provider function, chat() takes precedence. common argument supported chosen provider, chat() raises error rather silently ignoring . provider_capabilities() (see “Checking Provider Supports” ) lists arguments provider accepts.
code: # Common args in the verb llm_message("Write a haiku about tidyllm.") |>   chat(ollama(), .temperature = 0)  # Provider-specific args in the provider llm_message("Hello") |>   chat(ollama(.ollama_server = Sys.getenv("OLLAMA_SERVER")), .temperature = 0)

title: Get Started
text: Define R functions model can call conversation. Wrap tidyllm_tool(): tool provided, model can request execution, tidyllm runs R session, result fed back automatically. Multi-turn tool loops (model makes several tool calls) handled transparently.
code: get_current_time <- function(tz, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") {   format(Sys.time(), tz = tz, format = format, usetz = TRUE) }  time_tool <- tidyllm_tool(   .f          = get_current_time,   .description = "Returns the current time in a specified timezone.",   tz     = field_chr("The timezone identifier, e.g. 'Europe/Berlin'."),   format = field_chr("strftime format string. Default: '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'.") )  llm_message("What time is it in Stuttgart right now?") |>   chat(openai(), .tools = time_tool) ## Message History: ## system: ## You are a helpful assistant ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## user: ## What time is it in Stuttgart right now? ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## assistant: ## The current time in Stuttgart (Europe/Berlin) is 2025-03-03 ## 09:51:22 CET. ## --------------------------------------------------------------

text: Batch APIs (Claude, OpenAI, Mistral, Groq, Gemini) process large numbers requests overnight roughly half cost standard calls. Use send_batch() submit, check_batch() poll status, fetch_batch() retrieve results: get_reply(), get_reply_data() get_metadata() read whole list . schema, get_reply_data(conversations) returns tibble one row per reply; request failed keeps row, message error column. check_job() fetch_job() type-dispatching aliases; work batch objects background research jobs (see deep_research() ).
code: # Submit a batch and save the job handle to disk glue::glue("Write a poem about {x}", x = c("cats", "dogs", "hamsters")) |>   purrr::map(llm_message) |>   send_batch(claude()) |>   saveRDS("claude_batch.rds") # Check status readRDS("claude_batch.rds") |>   check_batch(claude()) ## # A tibble: 1 × 8 ##   batch_id          status created_at          expires_at          req_succeeded ##   <chr>             <chr>  <dttm>              <dttm>                      <int> ## 1 msgbatch_02A1B2C… ended  2025-11-01 10:30:00 2025-11-02 10:30:00             3 ## # ℹ 3 more variables: req_errored <int>, req_expired <int>, req_canceled <int> # Fetch completed results conversations <- readRDS("claude_batch.rds") |>   fetch_batch(claude())  poems <- get_reply(conversations)

We exploit three key features in this setting: i) investment in high-speed rail has, in some cases dramatically, reduced travel times between regions, ii) several small towns were connected to the high-speed rail network only for political reasons, and iii) high-speed trains have left the transportation of goods unaffected. Combining novel information on train schedules and the opening of high-speed rail stations with panel data on all workers in Germany, we show that a reduction in travel time by one percent raises the number of commuters between regions by 0.25 percent. This effect is mainly driven by workers changing jobs to smaller cities while keeping their place of residence in larger ones. Our findings support the notion that benefits from infrastructure investments accrue in particular to peripheral regions, which gain access to a large pool of qualified workers with a preference for urban life. We find that the introduction of high-speed trains led to a modal shift towards rail transportation in particular on medium distances between 150 and 400 kilometers."

code: library(here)  generate_abstract_embeddings <- function(abstracts) {   embedding_batches <- tibble(abstract = abstracts) |>     group_by(batch = floor(1:n() / 200) + 1) |>     group_split()    n_batches <- length(embedding_batches)   glue("Processing {n_batches} batches of 200 abstracts") |> cat("\n")    embedding_batches |>     walk(\(batch) {       batch_number <- pull(batch, batch) |> unique()       glue("Generate Text Embeddings for Abstract Batch: {batch_number}/{n_batches}") |> cat("\n")        batch$abstract |>         embed(ollama(.model = "mxbai-embed-large:latest")) |>         write_rds(here("embedded_abstracts", paste0(batch_number, ".rds")))     }) }  abstracts |>   pull(abstract) |>   generate_abstract_embeddings() ## Processing 115 batches of 200 abstracts ## Generate Text Embeddings for Abstract Batch: 1/115 ## Generate Text Embeddings for Abstract Batch: 2/115 ## Generate Text Embeddings for Abstract Batch: 3/115 ## ... embedded_abstracts <- here("embedded_abstracts") |>   dir() |>   map_dfr(\(f) read_rds(here("embedded_abstracts", f)))

text: embeddings precomputed, perform semantic search using cosine similarity. Cosine similarity measures similarity two vectors computing cosine angle ; ranges -1 (opposite directions) 1 (identical directions): cosine_similarity(𝐚,𝐛)=∑=1naibi∑=1nai2⋅∑=1nbi2 \text{cosine\_similarity}(\mathbf{}, \mathbf{b}) = \frac{\sum_{=1}^n a_i b_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^n a_i^2} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_{=1}^n b_i^2}} Vectors 90 degrees (orthogonal, semantic overlap) cosine similarity 0; vectors pointing direction similarity close 1. express simple function: apply find 10 similar abstracts corpus: ten similar articles corpus: Top 10 Similar Abstracts Unsurprisingly, top result target abstract . remaining results strongly align target’s focus transportation infrastructure economic effects; second result discusses German high-speed rail, third fourth cover Japan’s Shinkansen China’s HSR network. illustrates model’s ability capture semantic connections across diverse geographic policy contexts.
code: cosine_similarity <- function(a, b) {   sum(a * b) / (sqrt(sum(a^2)) * sqrt(sum(b^2))) } top10_similar <- embedded_abstracts |>   mutate(cosine_sim = map_dbl(embeddings,                               \(e) cosine_similarity(e, target_tbl$embeddings[[1]]))) |>   arrange(desc(cosine_sim)) |>   slice(1:10) |>   rename(abstract = input) |>   left_join(abstracts |> select(year, authors, journal, abstract), by = "abstract") |>   select(-embeddings)

Passing list tools lets model choose one call step.
code: get_country_capital <- function(country) {   capitals <- c(     France  = "Paris",     Germany = "Berlin",     Japan   = "Tokyo",     Brazil  = "Brasilia"   )   unname(capitals[country]) %||% "Unknown" }  get_city_population <- function(city) {   populations <- c(     Paris    = "2.1 million (city), 12 million (metro)",     Berlin   = "3.7 million (city), 6 million (metro)",     Tokyo    = "14 million (city), 37 million (metro)",     Brasilia = "3.1 million (city)"   )   unname(populations[city]) %||% "Unknown" }  capital_tool <- tidyllm_tool(   .f           = get_country_capital,   .description = "Return the capital city of a country.",   country      = field_chr("Country name, e.g. 'France'.") )  population_tool <- tidyllm_tool(   .f           = get_city_population,   .description = "Return the population of a city.",   city         = field_chr("City name, e.g. 'Paris'.") )  llm_message("What is the population of the capital of Japan?") |>   chat(openai(), .tools = list(capital_tool, population_tool), .max_tool_rounds = 5) ## Message History: ## system: ## You are a helpful assistant ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## user: ## What is the population of the capital of Japan? ## -------------------------------------------------------------- ## assistant: ## The capital of Japan is **Tokyo**. Its population is ## approximately 14 million people in the city proper and ## around 37 million in the greater metropolitan area, making ## it the most populous metropolitan area in the world. ## --------------------------------------------------------------

text: .llm LLMMessage object containing conversation history system prompt. .model Character string specifying Claude model version (default: "claude-sonnet-5-5"). .max_tokens Integer specifying maximum number tokens response (default: 1024). .temperature Numeric 0 1 controlling response randomness. supported older models; Claude Sonnet 5 Opus 4.7 newer reject sampling parameters. .top_k Integer controlling diversity limiting top K tokens. supported older models. .top_p Numeric 0 1 nucleus sampling. supported older models. .metadata List additional metadata include request. .stop_sequences Character vector sequences halt response generation. .tools List additional tools functions model can use. .json_schema schema enforce output structure .file_ids Character; vector file IDs files uploaded Anthropics Servers .api_url Base URL Anthropic API (default: "https://api.anthropic.com/"). .verbose Logical; TRUE, displays additional information API call (default: FALSE). .max_tries Maximum retries peform request .timeout Integer specifying request timeout seconds (default: 60). .stream Logical; TRUE, streams response piece piece (default: FALSE). .dry_run Logical; TRUE, returns prepared request object without executing (default: FALSE). .thinking Logical; TRUE, enables Claude's thinking mode. Claude Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6 newer maps adaptive thinking; older models uses fixed thinking budget (default: FALSE). .thinking_budget Integer specifying maximum tokens Claude can spend thinking (default: 1024). Must least 1024. used older models; ignored model supports adaptive thinking, .effort controls thinking depth instead. .effort Character; one "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max". Controls thinking depth overall token spend models support effort parameter (Claude Opus 4.5 newer, Claude Sonnet 4.6 newer). Default NULL uses API default ("high"). .cache Logical character; enables Anthropic prompt caching request. TRUE caches default 5-minute time live; "1h" requests one-hour time live. Cache reads cost roughly tenth base input price. Cache token counts reported get_metadata() cached_tokens cache_creation_tokens columns, raw form api_specific cache_creation_input_tokens cache_read_input_tokens (default: FALSE). Anthropic caches prompts per-model minimum, minimum higher cheaper models: 4096 tokens Haiku 4.5, 1024 Sonnet 5 Sonnet 4.6, 512 Opus 5. Shorter prompts error; simply report zero cache tokens. .max_tool_rounds Integer specifying maximum number tool use iterations (default: 10). Set 1 single-round tool use, higher multi-turn agentic loops.

title: Send LLM Messages to the DeepSeek Chat API — deepseek_chat
text: .llm LLMMessage object containing conversation history. .model identifier model use (default: "deepseek-v4-pro"). Use "deepseek-flash", alias latest Flash model, faster, cheaper alternative. .thinking TRUE, enables thinking mode via thinking: {type: "enabled"} request body captures reasoning trace metadata (default: NULL). Supported V4 models; note temperature, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty ignored thinking active. .max_tokens maximum number tokens can generated response (default: 2048). .temperature Controls randomness model's response. Values 0 2 allowed (optional). .top_p Nucleus sampling parameter controls proportion probability mass considered (optional). .frequency_penalty Number -2.0 2.0. Penalizes repeated tokens reduce repetition (optional). .presence_penalty Number -2.0 2.0. Encourages new topics penalizing tokens appeared far (optional). .stop One sequences API stop generating tokens (optional). .stream Logical; TRUE, streams response piece piece (default: FALSE). .logprobs TRUE, returns log probabilities output token (default: FALSE). .top_logprobs Number 0 5 specifying number top log probabilities return (optional). .tools Either single TOOL object list TOOL objects representing available functions tool calls. .tool_choice character string specifying tool-calling behavior; valid values "none", "auto", "required" (optional). .api_url Base URL DeepSeek API (default: "https://api.deepseek.com/"). .timeout Request timeout seconds (default: 60). .verbose TRUE, displays additional information API call (default: FALSE). .dry_run TRUE, returns constructed request object without executing (default: FALSE). .max_tries Maximum retries perform request (default: 3). .max_tool_rounds Integer specifying maximum number tool use iterations (default: 10). Set 1 single-round tool use, higher multi-turn agentic loops.

text: .llm LLMMessage object containing conversation history. .model model name (default: "local-model"). llama.cpp ignores value serves whatever GGUF loaded; default clear placeholder. .max_tokens Maximum tokens response (default: 1024). .temperature Controls randomness (0–2, optional). .top_p Nucleus sampling parameter (0–1, optional). .stop One stop sequences (optional). .stream Logical; TRUE, streams response (default: FALSE). .tools Either single TOOL object list TOOL objects. .tool_choice Tool-calling behavior: "none", "auto", "required" (optional). .json_schema JSON schema R list enforce structured output. Passed response_format = {type: "json_schema", ...} — enforced sampler level. .grammar BNF grammar string constrain sampling formal language (e.g. "root ::= [0-9]{4}" 4-digit year). Takes precedence .json_schema set; use one . .logprobs Logical; TRUE, returns token log-probabilities (default: FALSE). .top_logprobs Integer; number top-alternative log-prob entries return per token (1–20, optional). Requires .logprobs = TRUE. .seed Integer; random seed reproducible outputs (optional). .thinking Logical; TRUE, enables extended reasoning/thinking mode models support (e.g. Qwen3). NULL (default) lets server decide; FALSE explicitly disables faster responses; TRUE forces . thinking trace accessible via get_metadata(result)$api_specific$thinking. .thinking_budget Integer; maximum tokens model may use thinking .thinking = TRUE. NULL uses server default (optional). .server Base URL llama.cpp server. Defaults LLAMACPP_SERVER environment variable, falling back "http://localhost:9931". .api_key API key llama.cpp server. Defaults LLAMACPP_API_KEY environment variable. Leave unset server started without --api-key. .timeout Request timeout seconds (default: 120). .verbose TRUE, displays additional information (default: FALSE). .dry_run TRUE, returns request object without executing (default: FALSE). .max_tries Maximum retries (default: 3). .max_tool_rounds Maximum tool use iterations (default: 10).

Supported values vary model: mistral-large-4 accepts "low", "medium" "high", always reasons, rejects "none". .timeout connection time seconds (default: 120). .max_tries Maximum retries peform request .dry_run TRUE, perform dry run return request object (default: FALSE). .verbose additional information shown API call? (default: FALSE) .tools Either single TOOL object list TOOL objects representing available functions tool calls. .tool_choice character string specifying tool-calling behavior; valid values "none", "auto", "required". .max_tool_rounds Integer specifying maximum number tool use iterations (default: 10). Nothing runs thread second process. request driven R’s event loop, waiting curl’s file descriptors rather timer, gaps whatever else session . Two consequences follow worth knowing: several jobs run genuinely concurrently, blocking call pauses duration. Requires later package, promises well .stream = FALSE. Neither new hard dependency; checked point use. what: Streaming and tool calls work together
title: tidyllm 0.6.0
text: .stream = TRUE .tools used mutually exclusive: every provider raised “Streaming supported requests tool calls” given. restriction gone claude(), openai(), gemini(), ollama(), groq(), mistral(), deepseek(), openrouter(), llamacpp(), azure_openai() chat_completions(). reply streams console, tool calls run stream ends, follow-round streams . reason blocked tool loop reads tool calls complete response body, stream never produced; produced list events instead. new assemble_stream_body() generic folds events back body shape, has_tool_calls(), extract_tool_calls(), run_tool_calls() append_tool_messages() reused without single streaming-specific branch. Streamed blocking responses now carry raw$content, also async driver needs. Claude requires real reassembly: streams tool arguments JSON fragments split mid-token interleave two concurrent calls, accumulated per content block rather one buffer. OpenAI’s response.completed event already carries fully-formed calls, Gemini Ollama send calls parsed. Details worth knowing, cases exist two can now combined: streamed reply whose tool call cut max_tokens mid-arguments longer raises. partial arguments dropped turn ends stop_reason, reply user already watched arrive thrown away. Claude’s thinking blocks signatures survive assembly, .thinking = TRUE works together .stream .tools. Built-tools claude_websearch() keep arguments . Streamed logprobs still work. used read separate branch walked per-chunk deltas; now collected place blocking response carries , transports take one path. provider streams assembler raises rather silently skipping tools returning model’s preamble answer.

title: tidyllm 0.6.0
text: Nothing user-visible changed , largest structural change release. Every *_chat() used one function body welding request construction, HTTP call, tool loop add_message() together, meant nothing *_chat() reach middle . Twelve providers now split <provider>_build_chat_request() plus thin wrapper. builder returns everything response handling needs; shared finish_chat_response() runs tool loop, extracts reply metadata, tracks rate limits appends message. Whether request streams decided build time rather perform time, every provider commits streaming request : Gemini URL path, rest request body. .dry_run = TRUE still returns bare httr2 request, unchanged. ratelimit_from_header() parse_logprobs() gained APIProvider default returning NULL, providers inherit method use override back. Whether provider reports rate limits logprobs now property class rather flag call site set correctly. new api_compatible class covers chat_completions(.compatible = TRUE), third-party endpoint speaking OpenAI dialect return OpenAI’s rate limit headers. interpret_chat_response() splits response interpretation away transport, driver holding response req_perform_promise() req_perform_parallel() can reach handling blocking path uses. streamed response now interpreted exactly code blocking one. extract_metadata_stream(), generic six methods, gone: assemble_stream_body() turns events response body, reply comes parse_chat_response() metadata extract_metadata(), streaming branch ends interpret_chat_response() like every path. Beyond deleting duplicate, makes incomplete assembler detectable: reply used come pump’s text accumulator, assembler drop content plain streaming test notice. process_tool_loop() performs follow-rounds closure caller supplies rather calling perform_chat_request() . business deciding round performed, deciding twice made openai_chat(.stateful = TRUE) apply retry opening request (see bug fixes ). also seam event-loop driver needs, hand non-blocking performer. Streamed gemini() metadata therefore reports api_specific fields blocking call: cachedContentTokenCount, avgLogprobs groundingMetadata appear, streaming-token_details entry (copy raw usageMetadata) gone. Token counts, finishReason thinking_tokens unchanged.

title: tidyllm 0.6.0
text: pdf_page_batch(.page_range=) rendered wrong pages. text subset requested range images rendered position within subset, .page_range = c(3, 5) paired page 3’s text page 1’s image. page numbers now carried whole function. pdf_page_batch() returns named list, page_1, page_2 , numbers original document. parallel_chat() preserves names, reply can now traced back page. verb provider implement says . send_chat() chat_ellmer() used fail generic complaint unsupported arguments; now names verb provider explains chat_ellmer() hands conversation ellmer Chat object rather building request, nothing tidyllm stream. holds parallel_chat(), verb/provider pair never registered. Deprecation warnings claude(.file_ids=) gemini(.fileid=) longer tell user feature “likely used tidyllm package” ask file issue. pipeline split moved calls one frame deeper, changed lifecycle resolved calling environment. openai_chat(.stateful = TRUE) recovers expired server-side context request turn, just first. round tool loop used bypass retry entirely, context expired mid-conversation failed outright. rebuild still attempted opening request, now says : body reconstructs conversation stood turn began, using later discard tool calls results exchanged since. round falls back also tells loop request actually sent, next round builds one. perplexity() attaches search results metadata . hook read response object rather parsed body inside , get_metadata()$api_specific$search_results always NULL. Streamed replies carry , since assembler now merges Perplexity’s response-level search_results citations fields.

title: tidyllm 0.6.0
text: Every provider now streams one shared pump. six hand-rolled repeat loops gone; provider customises streaming implementing parse_stream_event() declaring stream_transport, never writing another loop. truncated abnormally terminated stream raises instead hanging. old loops relied solely provider-specific terminal event, closed connection, mid-stream provider error unrecognised finish_reason span forever. pump checks resp_stream_is_complete() every empty read. Measured change, openai(), claude() whole ChatCompletions family hung; providers now raise. .timeout finally applies streaming, idle deadline events rather total, long generation killed long. streaming path previously timeout backstop . perplexity() streams now terminate finish_reason, "stop"; reply cut short "length" used spin. gemini() streaming moved alt=sse endpoint. Without query parameter endpoint returns pretty-printed JSON array chunks SSE framing, tidyllm buffered text pattern matched . Gemini streaming metadata now reports finishReason thinking_tokens alongside token counts. Thinking deltas distinguished reply text every provider emits , rather concatenated reply dropped silently. console path opens connection blocking = TRUE instead spinning empty reads. Output unchanged; cadence may differ slightly, Ollama longer needs 0.25s sleep per line.

title: tidyllm 0.6.0
text: gemini() longer puts API key URL query string. fifteen Gemini request builders now send redacted x-goog-api-key header, .dry_run = TRUE, req_verbose() httr2 error carrying URL longer print live key. azure_openai() marks api-key header redacted. stored ordinary string, key survived print() serialize() request object.

title: tidyllm 0.6.0
text: chat_completions() reached chat() common argument ; chat(..., .dry_run = TRUE) every shared argument raised “supported provider’s chat() function”. Provider functions forward ... now recognised accepting common argument. missing API key raised object 'api' found instead intended instruction naming environment variable set. chat_ellmer() sent last user message twice. full history, including final user turn, written onto cloned ellmer Chat turn sent $chat(). now sets preceding turns, uses ellmer’s public $set_turns() rather reaching object’s private environment. chat_ellmer() accepted .stream = TRUE silently performed non-streaming request. now streams ellmer’s $stream(), get_metadata() reports stream = TRUE replies. claude_chat() ignored .max_tries always used default 3. ollama_chat() gains .max_tries, hardcoded 3. Ollama stream loop longer crashes JSON lexer error empty read, raises instead looping connection completes model reports done. ChatCompletions stream loop recorded last event twice. duplicate gone final usage-chunk now recorded produced rather [DONE] branch. pdf_page_batch() longer emits one deprecation warning per page; uses .media = img() instead deprecated .imagefile. Deleted duplicate openai chatgpt bindings R/api_chat_completions.R, shipped dead code shadowed Responses API definitions. Deleted generate_callback_function() generic, wrote environment never created errored called. R/api_ellmer.R longer short-circuits top level ellmer absent, broken NAMESPACE exports; chat_ellmer() checks ellmer call time instead.

title: tidyllm 0.5.2

what: JSON schemas (structured output and tool definitions)
title: tidyllm 0.5.2
text: tidyllm_schema() now sets additionalProperties: false every object node assembled schema, just root. Schemas containing field_object(..., .vector = TRUE), .e. array objects, rejected HTTP 400 invalid_json_schema every provider enforcing OpenAI strict mode: openai() openrouter() route OpenAI Azure. recursive normalization applied provider boundary, raw list schemas ellmer types covered well. gemini() strips additionalProperties recursively sending schema. Gemini rejects key node, previously root stripped. Tool definitions get treatment. tidyllm_tool() field_object() argument produced nested object node without additionalProperties, openai() rejected 400 tidyllm sends strict = TRUE tool schemas. schema name now read attr(..., exact = TRUE). Passing hand-written list schema without name attribute previously partial-matched names attribute, property names went wire schema name strict providers rejected request. Note explicit additionalProperties = TRUE, instance ellmer::type_object(.additional_properties = TRUE), now normalized FALSE, since strict mode requires.

title: tidyllm 0.5.2
text: Provider errors coming OpenAI-compatible gateway longer empty. openrouter() reports generic "Provider returned error" error$message keeps real upstream diagnostic error$metadata$raw; tidyllm now unwraps payload names upstream provider error raises. made schema bug hard diagnose field. applies whole ChatCompletions family azure_openai(). error type falls back error$code provider reports error$type, error header longer Type: NULL.

title: tidyllm 0.5.2
text: get_metadata() gains two top-level columns: cached_tokens (prompt tokens served provider’s cache, billing-relevant number) cache_creation_tokens (cache writes; Claude ). Providers report cache usage return NA_integer_, “caching” “cache miss” stay distinguishable. Raw provider fields remain api_specific, existing code keeps working. Cache counts now read previously discarded: openai() (Responses API), gemini(), deepseek(), chat_ellmer(), whole ChatCompletions family including openrouter(). openrouter() additionally reports cache_discount api_specific. gemini() groq() replies now report stream = FALSE instead NA, metadata tibble mixing providers consistent. Claude streaming metadata longer stub. Streamed replies now report stop_reason, id, stop_sequence, cache tokens thinking trace, matching non-streaming path.

title: tidyllm 0.5.2
text: gemini() tool calls work . Gemini now rejects functionCall part whose thoughtSignature dropped (“Function call missing thought_signature”), broke every multi-round tool call. tidyllm sends model’s parts back verbatim. claude_websearch() defaults current web_search_20260318 tool version gains .allowed_callers .response_inclusion. Since web_search_20260209 API defaults allowed_callers code execution tool, models programmatic tool calling support; web search therefore failed 400 Claude Haiku 4.5 older models. tidyllm now sends allowed_callers = "direct" default, web search works every model . Pass .allowed_callers = "code_execution_20260120" dynamic filtering path. ellmer_tool() longer produces tidyllm_field whose type carries stray name, uses built-tool’s description ellmer provides one. ellmer now declared Suggests: ellmer (>= 0.4.0), version tidyllm’s tool conversion actually requires. .cache documentation claude_chat() now states per-model minimum cacheable prompt length. Anthropic silently caches nothing floor, floor higher cheap models (4096 tokens Haiku 4.5) Sonnet 5 (1024).

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: CRAN release: 2026-04-30

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: non-text content now attaches messages single .media argument accepts combination media types. Pass single object list:
code: # Single image llm_message("What is in this image?",             .media = img("photo.jpg")) |>   chat(claude())  # Multiple images in one message llm_message("Describe the difference between these two images.",             .media = list(img("before.jpg"), img("after.jpg"))) |>   chat(openai())  # Mixed types: image + PDF together llm_message("Does this figure match what is reported in Table 2?",             .media = list(img("figure_3.png"),                           pdf_file("paper.pdf", pages = 1:8))) |>   chat(gemini())

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: Three new constructors join img(): audio_file(path): attach audio inline; supported gemini(), openrouter(), mistral() (Voxtral models) video_file(path): attach video inline; supported gemini() openrouter() pdf_file(path, pages, .text_extract): attach PDF; Claude Gemini receive binary file (preserving layout, tables, scanned content); providers receive extracted text automatically
code: # Transcribe a recording llm_message("Summarise what is discussed in this interview.",             .media = audio_file("bosch_interview.mp3")) |>   chat(gemini())  # Analyse a video clip with a JSON schema video_schema <- tidyllm_schema(   title      = field_chr("Title or subject of the clip"),   era        = field_chr("Approximate decade or period depicted"),   key_people = field_chr("Names mentioned, semicolon-separated") )  llm_message("Analyse this video clip.",             .media = video_file("documentary.mp4")) |>   chat(gemini(), .json_schema = video_schema)  # Extract references from a scanned PDF (binary path, no OCR needed) llm_message("Extract all references in APA format.",             .media = pdf_file("1995_Neal_Industry_Specific.pdf")) |>   chat(claude(), .json_schema = ref_schema)  # Force text extraction for any provider llm_message("Summarise this report.",             .media = pdf_file("annual_report.pdf", .text_extract = TRUE)) |>   chat(openai())

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: providers accept images now handle multiple images per message. Pass list inside .media. Claude supports 600 images per message; Gemini 3,600.

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: unified set verbs manages files stored provider servers. Upload , reuse across many requests: pattern works claude() openai(). Provider support: Gemini: PDFs, images, audio, video, plain text, CSV, HTML, ; files expire 48 hours Claude: PDFs images; automatic expiry OpenAI: 80+ formats including PDFs, Office documents (DOCX, PPTX, XLSX), source code, ZIP archives, images; note images uploaded via Files API used vision tasks chat; use inline img() instead tidyllm_file provider-specific: file uploaded Claude sent Gemini. tidyllm validates provider match every request.
code: # Upload; returns a tidyllm_file handle report <- upload_file(gemini(), .path = "quarterly_report.pdf")  # Attach the handle to any message via .files llm_message("What were the key results this quarter?",             .files = report) |>   chat(gemini())  llm_message("List the top three risks in the document.",             .files = report) |>   chat(gemini())  # Inspect and manage uploaded files list_files(gemini()) file_info(gemini(), report)      # accepts a tidyllm_file or a plain ID string delete_file(gemini(), report)

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: openai() now uses Responses API (POST /v1/responses). existing workflows continue work unchanged. New capabilities unlocked rewrite: Batch processing (send_batch(openai())) continues use Chat Completions endpoint internally.
code: # Reasoning effort for o-series models llm_message("Prove that there are infinitely many primes.") |>   chat(openai(.model = "o4-mini"), .reasoning_effort = "high")  # Stateful multi-turn conversations (server retains context by ID) first  <- llm_message("My name is Alex.") |>   chat(openai(), .stateful = TRUE)  second <- llm_message("What is my name?") |>   chat(openai(), .previous_response_id = first)

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
code: # Web search: the server runs the search, results appear in the reply llm_message("What happened in AI research this week?") |>   chat(openai(), .tools = openai_websearch())  # Code interpreter llm_message("Plot a histogram of 1,000 standard-normal samples.") |>   chat(openai(), .tools = openai_code_interpreter())  # Mix built-in and custom tools in one call llm_message("Find today's EUR/USD rate and convert 500 EUR.") |>   chat(openai(), .tools = list(openai_websearch(), my_converter_tool))

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
code: # Background research job (slow; typically 5 to 30 minutes) job <- llm_message("Survey the literature on causal inference with LLMs.") |>   deep_research(openai(.model = "o4-mini-deep-research"), .background = TRUE)  check_job(job) result <- fetch_job(job)

title: tidyllm 0.5.0
text: chat_completions() provider OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, LiteLLM, Together AI, Anyscale, others), without repurpose openai():
code: llm_message("Hello!") |>   chat(chat_completions(     .api_url        = "https://api.together.xyz/v1/",     .api_key_env_var = "TOGETHER_API_KEY",     .model          = "meta-llama/Llama-3-8b-chat-hf"   ))

title: tidyllm 0.4.0
text: Full support local llama.cpp servers, including chat, embeddings, reranking, model management:
code: # Chat with a local llama.cpp server llm_message("Explain R to a Python developer") |>   chat(llamacpp())  # Generate embeddings c("text one", "text two") |> embed(llamacpp())  # Rerank documents by relevance llamacpp_rerank("best R package for LLMs", c("tidyllm", "ellmer", "httr2"))  # Model management llamacpp_list_local_models()          # list models in the model directory list_hf_gguf_files("Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-GGUF")  # browse HuggingFace GGUF files llamacpp_download_model("Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-GGUF", "qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf") llamacpp_delete_model("path/to/model.gguf") llamacpp_health()                     # check server status

code: # Blocking — waits for completion and returns an LLMMessage result <- llm_message("Compare Rust and Go for systems programming") |>   deep_research(perplexity())  get_reply(result) get_metadata(result)$api_specific[[1]]$citations  # Background — returns immediately, poll with check_job() / fetch_job() job <- llm_message("Summarize the latest EU AI Act developments") |>   deep_research(perplexity(), .background = TRUE)  check_job(job)   # poll status result <- fetch_job(job)  # retrieve when complete

title: Version 0.3.4
text: CRAN release: 2025-03-27 release marks major internal refactor accompanied suite subtle yet impactful improvements. many changes occur hood, collectively deliver robust, flexible, maintainable framework.

title: Version 0.3.4
text: Robust Streaming: New Streaming Backend: Streaming now handled via httr2::req_perform_connection() (httr2 ≥ 1.1.1), resulting stable reliable experience. Metadata Streaming: Streaming requests now also support metadata extraction, logprobs, features, making even informative. Optimized Internal Processing: S7 Methods Integration: Improved handling streams chat parsing using proper S7 methods instead clunky old function generation. OpenAI Request Construction: OpenAI Azure OpenAI (along batch functions) now use common request construction function reduce code duplication simplify maintenance. Schema support: New field_object() function allow nested schemata Expanded API Features: mistral() now accepts .json_schema argument. claude() incorporates .json_schema via JSON-extractor tool, line Anthropic’s guidelines. Batch API groq(): new batch processing interface implemented groq().

title: Dev-Version 0.3.3
text: Claude now supports reasoning:
code: conversation <- llm_message("Are there an infinite number of prime numbers such that n mod 4 == 3?") |>    chat(claude(.thinking=TRUE)) |>   print()     #> Message History: #> system: #> You are a helpful assistant #> -------------------------------------------------------------- #> user: #> Are there an infinite number of prime numbers such that n #> mod 4 == 3? #> -------------------------------------------------------------- #> assistant: #> # Infinitude of Primes Congruent to 3 mod 4 #>  #> Yes, there are infinitely many prime numbers $p$ such #> that $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ (when $p$ divided by 4 leaves #> remainder 3). #>  #> ## Proof by Contradiction #>  #> I'll use a proof technique similar to Euclid's classic proof #> of the infinitude of primes: #>  #> 1) Assume there are only finitely many primes $p$ such that #> $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. Let's call them $p_1, p_2, ..., p_k$. #>  #> 2) Consider the number $N = 4p_1p_2...p_k - 1$ #>  #> 3) Note that $N \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ since $4p_1p_2...p_k #> \equiv 0 \pmod{4}$ and $4p_1p_2...p_k - 1 \equiv -1 \equiv 3 #> \pmod{4}$ #>  #> 4) $N$ must have at least one prime factor $q$ #>  #> 5) For any $i$ between 1 and $k$, we have $N \equiv -1 #> \pmod{p_i}$, so $N$ is not divisible by any of the primes #> $p_1, p_2, ..., p_k$ #>  #> 6) Therefore, $q$ is a prime not in our original list #>  #> 7) Furthermore, $q$ must be congruent to 3 modulo 4: #> - $q$ cannot be 2 because $N$ is odd #> - If $q \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, then $\frac{N}{q} \equiv 3 #> \pmod{4}$ would need another prime factor congruent to 3 #> modulo 4 #> - So $q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ #>  #> 8) This contradicts our assumption that we listed all primes #> of the form $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ #>  #> Therefore, there must be infinitely many primes of the form #> $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. #> --------------------------------------------------------------  #Thinking process is stored in API-specific metadata conversation |>     get_metadata() |>    dplyr::pull(api_specific) |>    purrr::map_chr("thinking") |>    cat()     #> The question is asking if there are infinitely many prime numbers $p$ such that $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, i.e., when divided by 4, the remainder is 3. #>  #> I know that there are infinitely many prime numbers overall. The classic proof is Euclid's proof by contradiction: if there were only finitely many primes, we could multiply them all together, add 1, and get a new number not divisible by any of the existing primes, which gives us a contradiction. #>  #> For primes of the form $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, we can use a similar proof strategy.  #>  #> Let's assume there are only finitely many primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$ such that $p_i \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ for all $i$.  #>  #> Now, consider the number $N = 4 \cdot p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_k - 1$.  #>  #> Note that $N \equiv -1 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.  #>  #> Now, let's consider the prime factorization of $N$. If $N$ is itself prime, then we have found a new prime $N$ such that $N \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, which contradicts our assumption that we enumerated all such primes. #>  > ...

title: Version 0.2.0
text: CRAN release: 2024-11-07 New CRAN release. Largest changes compared 0.1.0: Major Features: Batch Request Support: Added support batch requests Anthropic OpenAI APIs, enabling large-scale request handling. Schema Support: Improved structured outputs JSON mode advanced .json_schema handling openai(), enhancing support well-defined JSON responses. Azure OpenAI Integration: Introduced azure_openai() function accessing Azure OpenAI service, full support rate-limiting batch operations tailored Azure’s API structure. Embedding Model Support: Added embedding generation functions OpenAI, Ollama, Mistral APIs, supporting message content media embedding. Mistral API Integration: New mistral() function provides full support Mistral models hosted EU, including rate-limiting streaming capabilities. PDF Batch Processing: Introduced pdf_page_batch() function, processes PDFs page page, allowing users define page-specific prompts detailed analysis. Support OpenAI-compatible APIs: Introduced .compatible argument (flexible url path) openai() allow compatibility third-party OpenAI-compatible APIs. Improvements: API Format Refactoring: Complete refactor to_api_format() reduce code duplication, simplify API format generation, improve maintainability. Improved Error Handling: Enhanced input validation error messaging API-functions functions, making troubleshooting easier. Rate-Limiting Enhancements: Updated rate limiting use httr2::req_retry() addition rate-limit tracking functions tidyllm, using 429 headers wait rate limit resets. Expanded Testing: Added comprehensive tests API functions using httptest2 Breaking Changes: Redesigned Reply Functions: get_reply() split get_reply() text outputs get_reply_data() structured outputs, improving type stability compared earlier function different outputs based .json-arguement. Deprecation chatgpt(): chatgpt() function deprecated favor openai() feature alignment improved consistency. Minor Updates Bug Fixes: Expanded PDF Support llm_message(): Allows extraction specific page ranges PDFs, improving flexibility document handling. New ollama_download_model() function download models Ollama API sequential chat API functions now support streaming
